quote: but that there was a corresponding old Persian legend about the Babylonian gods Marduk and Ishtar, and the rival Elamite gods Humman and Vashti
content: The "archaeological evidence" is a nineteenth-century etymological conjecture that the field abandoned. Jensen proposed in 1892 that Mordecai and Esther derive from Marduk and Ishtar and Haman and Vashti from the Elamite deities Humban and Mashti, on the strength of name resemblances; there is no Persian legend of a conflict between these gods, "Vashti" as an Elamite goddess rests on a doubtful reading, and the standard commentaries treat the theory as historically interesting and unsupported (Moore, Esther, Anchor Bible, 1971, book, no DOI). The absence of Esther from Persian records is real and is the actual argument. The essay presents the woman as knowing the evidence against her religion, and the evidence it lists is a hypothesis that scholars of her own tradition and outside it had set aside decades before, which suggests that the conversation's expert on the historicity of Purim was not the author's interlocutor.

quote: She hasn’t actually deceived herself into believing that God exists or that the Jewish religion is true. Not even close, so far as I can tell.
content: The alternative to "she has failed to deceive herself" is that she is doing what religious belief usually is. The cognitive science of religion distinguishes factual belief from religious credence: credence is not evidentially vulnerable, is compartmentalized to practical and ceremonial settings, is expressed as "I believe in" rather than "there is," and is held together with an accurate factual map of the same world (Van Leeuwen 2014). Every observation the essay reports, the "I believe in God" phrasing, the talk of consequences of believing rather than of God, the agreement that an observer would not invent the hypothesis, is the signature of credence, and the Book I annotations traced the same pattern through Belief in Belief. The essay's conclusion, that only one attitude counts as belief and hers is not it, is a stipulation. What was discovered in those few hours is the ordinary structure of a religious mind, reported as an anomaly by an observer using one person, one conversation and no notes.
